q: 1. With the help of leveling we measures
explain: Leveling is used to determine the relative heights (vertical distances/angles) of points on the Earth's surface.

q: 2. Determining the difference in elevation between two points on the surface of the earth, is known as
explain: Leveling, in its most general definition, is the branch of surveying concerned with determining the difference in elevation between points on the earth's surface.

q: 3. Any arbitrarily assumed level line from which vertical distances are measured is known as
explain: A datum line (or datum surface) is the reference point or 'zero' from which all elevations in a survey are calculated.

q: 4. When the bubble of the level tube of level, remains central
options: axis of the telescope is horizontal
geometrical axis of the telescope is horizontal
explain: When the bubble is centred (in an adjusted level), the axis of the bubble tube is horizontal, which in turn means the line of sight is horizontal.

q: 5. The difference between a level line and a horizontal line is that
options: level line is normal to plumb line while horizontal line is not necessarily
level line is curved but horizontal line is a straight line
explain: A horizontal line is a straight line tangential to a level line at a specific point; a level line follows the Earth's curvature.

q: 6. During leveling the readings are generally taken by the level man. The staff man also takes the reading if the staff is a type of
explain: On a target staff, the level man directs the staff man to move a target until it aligns with the crosshairs, and then the staff man reads the value.

q: 7. A number of readings taken between back sight and fore sight are called
explain: These are technically called Intermediate Sights (IS). Since 'middle sight' isn't standard terminology, 'none of the above' is selected.

q: 8. A staff reading taken on a bench mark/known elevation or change point is known as
explain: The first reading taken after setting up the level, typically on a point of known elevation, is the Back Sight (BS).

q: 9. In levelling the station where back sight and fore sight readings are taken during the operation is known as
explain: A Change Point (CP) is a stable point on which both a Fore Sight and a Back Sight are taken to move the instrument forward.

q: 10. A relatively fixed point of known elevation above datum is called
explain: A Bench Mark (BM) is a permanent point of reference whose elevation with respect to a specific datum is known and used for leveling operations.

q: 11. An operation for determining the relative elevations of different points on the surface of the earth is known as
explain: Differential leveling is the method used to determine the difference in elevation between two points, regardless of the distance between them.

q: 12. In a dumpy level, the objective and eyepiece lenses are made of two or more small lenses to obtain
explain: Composite lenses are used to correct aberrations (chromatic and spherical), resulting in a sharp, distinct image and better light transmission.

q: 13. During levelling generally instrumental error is occuring due to
explain: Collimation error occurs when the line of sight is not truly horizontal even when the bubble is centered, which is a classic instrumental error.

q: 14. When bubble of the telescope is centered then
explain: In a perfectly adjusted level, centering the bubble ensures that the line of sight (axis of collimation) is truly horizontal.

q: 15. The image of the objectives formed should lie
options: in the plane of cross hairs
at the center of the eyepiece
at the optical center of the eyepiece.
explain: To eliminate parallax and take accurate readings, the image formed by the objective lens must coincide exactly with the plane of the cross-hairs.

q: 16. The absence of spherical aberration in a telescope is known as
explain: Aplanatism (or aplanation) refers to a lens system that is free from both spherical aberration and coma.

q: 17. Reading of the metric levelling staff can be taken accurately up to
explain: A metric levelling staff, graduated to 5 mm divisions, can be read accurately to about 0.01 m (10 mm) by estimation between graduations, or precisely to the smallest graduation.

q: 18. The absence of chromatic aberration in a telescope is known as
explain: Achromatism is the property of an optical system that eliminates chromatic aberration, allowing different wavelengths of light to focus at the same point.

q: 19. The combined correction due to refraction and earth's curvature is
explain: Since the curvature correction (negative, i.e., subtracted from the reading, or rather makes the object appear lower requiring a positive elevation correction) and refraction correction (positive, opposite in sign, smaller in magnitude) partly offset each other, but the net combined effect is applied as a subtractive correction to the staff reading.

q: 20. The magnification of a telescope depends upon
options: inverse of ratio of (b) and (a) above
explain: Magnifying power is defined by the ratio of the focal length of the objective ($f_o$) to the focal length of the eyepiece ($f_e$).

q: 21. The errors in levelling due to earths' curvature are
explain: The error introduced by the earth's curvature, if uncorrected, always makes the staff reading appear too great (object appears lower than actual), which is treated as a positive error in the observed reading.

q: 22. An arbitrary surface with reference to which the elevation of points are measured and compared, is called
explain: A datum surface is any arbitrarily chosen reference surface (such as mean sea level) from which elevations of points are measured and compared.

q: 23. In an internal focussing type of telescope, the negative lens provided is
explain: Internal focusing telescopes use a movable double concave (negative) lens located between the objective and the diaphragm.

q: 24. When it is not possible to set up the level, midway between the two points, then the difference in elevation between them is measured by
explain: Reciprocal levelling is specifically used when it is impossible to set the instrument midway between two points (e.g., across a river or ravine), allowing errors of curvature, refraction and collimation to be eliminated by observing from both ends.

q: 25. A line normal to the plumb line at all points is known as
explain: A level line is defined as a curved line that is normal (perpendicular) to the direction of the plumb line (gravity) at every point along its length.

q: 26. An inter focusing type of telescope is focused by the movement of
explain: In internal focusing, the objective and eyepiece remain fixed while a negative (concave) lens moves along the axis to focus.

q: 27. The combined correction for refraction and earth's curvature (in levelling observations) is
explain: The standard formula for combined correction for curvature and refraction (distance d in km) is 0.06735*d2 metres, obtained after applying the standard refraction coefficient to the pure curvature correction of 0.0785*d2.

q: 28. The sensitivity of the bubble tube can be increased by
options: decreasing the radius of curvature of tube
increasing the diameter of the tube
explain: Sensitivity increases with an increase in the radius of curvature, the length of the bubble, and the internal diameter of the tube.

q: 29. If the back sight and fore sight distance are kept equal during levelling observations, then the effect of both refraction and earth's curvature will be
explain: When back sight and fore sight distances are kept equal, the equal and opposite curvature/refraction errors in both readings cancel out exactly, giving a net effect of zero on the computed difference in level.

q: 30. A level tube is used to make line of sight horizontal. It is filled with
explain: Liquids like ether, alcohol, or chloroform are used because they have low viscosity and low freezing points, allowing the bubble to move quickly and freely.

q: 31. In a constant level tube, size of the bubble remains constant because upper wall of tube has
explain: A large radius of curvature in the upper wall allows for a more sensitive and stable bubble length despite minor temperature changes.

q: 32. Levelling across a river is done by
explain: Reciprocal levelling is the standard method used to determine the difference in elevation across an obstacle like a river, where the instrument cannot be set up midway.

q: 33. Reciprocal leveling eliminates
options: collimation and curvature error fully and refraction error partly
explain: Reciprocal leveling, by averaging observations taken from both ends of a line, eliminates the combined effects of collimation error, earth's curvature, and atmospheric refraction.

q: 34. If temperature increases the sensitivity of a bubble tube
explain: Increased temperature causes the liquid to expand, which decreases the length of the bubble and consequently its sensitivity.

q: 35. Sensitivity of a level tube is expressed by
options: length of bubble of level tube
explain: Sensitivity is mathematically related to the radius of curvature (R); the larger the radius, the more sensitive the tube.

q: 36. Dumpy level is used when
options: number of observation to be taken are large from one level position
number of observation to be taken are small from one level position
fly levelling is to be done
explain: Because the telescope is fixed to its supports, the Dumpy level is sturdy and efficient for taking many readings from a single setup.

q: 37. In a theodolite the line of collimation is
options: parallel to axis of plate levels
explain: For correct theodolite operation, the line of collimation must be perpendicular to the trunnion (horizontal) axis, so that it sweeps out a true vertical plane when the telescope is plunged.

q: 38. Automatic level has advantages of
options: freedom from errors and external influence
comfortable and has large range of application
explain: Automatic levels use a compensator to maintain a horizontal line of sight, making them faster, more precise, and more reliable than manual levels.

q: 39. Error in sighting and reading is termed as
explain: Errors arising from the limitations of the observer's own senses in sighting and reading (e.g., estimation errors) are classified as personal errors.

q: 40. The height of instrument method is
explain: The HI (Height of Instrument) method requires fewer calculations per point than the Rise and Fall method, making it faster for large numbers of intermediate sights.

q: 41. Height of instrument method of levelling as compared to rise and fall method is
explain: While less accurate in terms of self-checking intermediate sights, the HI method is significantly faster and easier to calculate.

q: 42. The rise and fall method of levelling provides a complete check on
explain: The Rise and Fall method has the advantage of checking all readings, including intermediate sights, ensuring the RL of every point is correct.

q: 43. The rise and fall method
options: provides a check on the intermediate readings
is preferable for differential and check levelling
explain: Due to its rigorous checking of all staff readings, it is the preferred method for high-precision engineering surveys.

q: 44. The curvature of the earth is taken into consideration if the limit of survey is
explain: As with Q1, surveys covering more than about 260 km2 must take the earth's curvature into account and are treated as geodetic surveys.

q: 45. If the observed reading of a level staff is 3.83 m, and at the point sighted the staff is 0.15 m off the vertical through the bottom, the correct reading will be
explain: Using the Pythagorean theorem, the true vertical height is $\sqrt{3.83^2 - 0.15^2} \approx 3.827$ m.

q: 46. A fixed point of reference of known elevation is called
explain: A bench mark (BM) is a fixed, stable point of known and recorded elevation used as a reference in leveling operations.

q: 47. The observed reading on a levelling staff was 3.545 m. If the staff was 0.150 m off from the original ground level, what should be correct reading?
explain: If the staff is held 0.150m away/down from the original point, the reading must be adjusted by subtraction (3.545 - 0.150 = 3.395m) to reflect the correct ground position.

q: 48. The observed reading on a levelling staff was 3.525 m. If the staff was 0.125m on from the original ground level, what should be correct reading?
explain: If the staff is on (elevated) by 0.125m, the ground reading is calculated by adding the offset: 3.525 + 0.125 = 3.65m.

q: 49. The levelling of instrument is done such that
options: line of sight is truly horizontal
line of collimation is truly horizontal
explain: The fundamental purpose of leveling the instrument base is to ensure the vertical axis is truly vertical, which allows the line of sight to sweep a horizontal plane.

q: 50. In case of leveling staff readings are taken by (In case of target staff)
explain: In target leveling, the instrument man signals the staff man to move the target; once aligned, the staff man reads the value from the staff.
